notes: Short source chapter — 9 Objective I items, all rebuilt, topped up to 10 with a resonance item. One source item asks which of four curves shows reactance against frequency; re-cast as a question about how each reactance varies.

practice_bank.title: Practice — Alternating Current
practice_bank.intro: Ten questions on a.c. circuits. The recurring idea: reactance depends on frequency, and that single fact drives filters, resonance and transformers alike.

sections.title: Reactance and Impedance
sections.blurb: Capacitors block low frequencies; inductors block high ones.

items.prompt: A capacitor acts as an infinite resistance for
items.explanation: Capacitive reactance is $ X_C = 1/\omega C $, which becomes infinite as $ \omega \to 0 $. So a capacitor blocks d.c. completely while passing a.c. — the higher the frequency the more freely. This is why capacitors are used to block d.c. while coupling a signal through.

items.prompt: As the frequency rises, the reactances of an inductor and a capacitor respectively
items.explanation: $ X_L = \omega L $ grows in proportion to frequency, while $ X_C = 1/\omega C $ falls inversely. They cross at the resonant frequency, where they cancel. This opposite behaviour is exactly what makes frequency-selective circuits possible.

items.prompt: A series a.c. circuit has resistance $ 4\ \Omega $ and reactance $ 3\ \Omega $. Its impedance is
items.explanation: Resistance and reactance are $ 90^\circ $ out of phase, so they combine as perpendicular vectors: $ Z = \sqrt{R^{2}+X^{2}} = \sqrt{16+9} = 5\ \Omega $. Adding them arithmetically to get $ 7\ \Omega $ ignores the phase difference and is the standard error.

items.prompt: An a.c. source producing $ E = E_0[\cos(100\pi t) + \cos(500\pi t)] $ drives a series $ RC $ circuit, giving currents of amplitude $ i_1 $ and $ i_2 $ at the two frequencies. Then
items.explanation: The higher frequency meets a smaller capacitive reactance, hence a smaller impedance, hence a larger current. Since $ 500\pi > 100\pi $, we get $ i_2 > i_1 $. An $ RC $ circuit therefore passes high frequencies preferentially — a high-pass filter.

sections.title: RMS and Peak Values
sections.blurb: What a meter reads, and what the insulation must withstand.

items.prompt: The peak voltage of a $ 220 $ V a.c. supply is about
items.explanation: Quoted a.c. voltages are rms values, and $ V_0 = \sqrt{2}\,V_{rms} = 1.414 \times 220 \approx 311 $ V. Insulation has to survive the *peak*, not the rms, which is why this distinction matters practically as well as numerically.

items.prompt: The rms value of the current $ i = i_0\sin\omega t $ is
items.explanation: Averaging $ i^{2} $ over a cycle gives $ i_0^{2}/2 $, whose square root is $ i_0/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707 i_0 $. The rms value is defined this way precisely so that $ i_{rms}^{2}R $ gives the true average power — the *mean* current over a cycle is zero and would be useless.

items.prompt: The average power consumed in a **purely inductive** a.c. circuit over a full cycle is
items.explanation: Current and voltage are exactly $ 90^\circ $ out of phase in a pure inductor, so the power factor $ \cos\phi $ is zero. Energy flows into the magnetic field for a quarter cycle and back out the next — a 'wattless' current. Only resistance dissipates energy.

sections.title: Transformers and Resonance
sections.blurb: Two applications that only a.c. makes possible.

options: in both a.c. and d.c. circuits
items.explanation: A transformer works by mutual induction, which requires a *changing* flux. Steady d.c. gives $ di/dt = 0 $ and induces nothing in the secondary. This inability to transform d.c. voltages is the reason electrical grids worldwide are a.c.

items.prompt: A step-up transformer raises the voltage. Ignoring losses, the current in the secondary compared with the primary is
items.explanation: Power is conserved, so $ V_p i_p = V_s i_s $ — raising the voltage must lower the current in proportion. This is why power is transmitted at high voltage: the same power travels as a smaller current, and $ i^{2}R $ losses in the cables fall as the square.

items.prompt: At resonance in a series $ LCR $ circuit,
options: the impedance is minimum and equals $ R $
items.explanation: At $ \omega = 1/\sqrt{LC} $ the two reactances cancel, leaving only $ R $. Impedance is therefore least, current greatest, and the power factor exactly 1 — voltage and current in phase. A *parallel* $ LCR $ circuit does the opposite, which is why it is used to reject a frequency rather than select it.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — RMS and peak values
worked_examples.problem: An a.c. supply is $ V = 311\sin(314t) $ volts. Find the rms voltage, the frequency and the period.
worked_examples.solution:
**Peak voltage:** $ V_0 = 311 $ V

**RMS voltage:**

$ V_{rms} = \frac{V_0}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{311}{1.414} = 220\ \text{V} $

**Angular frequency:** $ \omega = 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1} $, so

$ f = \frac{\omega}{2\pi} = \frac{314}{6.28} = 50\ \text{Hz} $

**Period:** $ T = 1/50 = 0.02 $ s

**These are exactly the Indian mains values** — $ 220 $ V rms at $ 50 $ Hz, with a peak of $ 311 $ V.

**Why rms is the useful measure.** It is the d.c. value that would deliver the same average power. A $ 220 $ V a.c. supply heats a resistor exactly as a $ 220 $ V battery would, even though its instantaneous voltage swings between $ \pm 311 $ V and passes through zero a hundred times a second.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Impedance of a series LCR circuit
worked_examples.problem: A series circuit has $ R = 30\ \Omega $, $ L = 0.2 $ H and $ C = 50\ \mu\text{F} $, driven at $ 50 $ Hz. Find the impedance and the current for a $ 220 $ V supply.
worked_examples.solution:
**Angular frequency:** $ \omega = 2\pi(50) = 314\ \text{rad s}^{-1} $

**Inductive reactance:**

$ X_L = \omega L = (314)(0.2) = 62.8\ \Omega $

**Capacitive reactance:**

$ X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{(314)(50 \times 10^{-6})} = \frac{1}{0.0157} = 63.7\ \Omega $

**Impedance:**

$ Z = \sqrt{R^{2} + (X_L - X_C)^{2}} = \sqrt{900 + (62.8-63.7)^{2}} = \sqrt{900 + 0.81} = 30.0\ \Omega $

**Current:**

$ i_{rms} = \frac{220}{30.0} = 7.33\ \text{A} $

**Note how nearly the reactances cancelled.** $ X_L $ and $ X_C $ differ by less than $ 1\ \Omega $, so this circuit is almost exactly at resonance — and the impedance has collapsed to essentially $ R $ alone.

**The subtraction, not addition, is the key point.** $ X_L $ and $ X_C $ are $ 180^\circ $ out of phase with each other, so they oppose. Adding them to get $ 126\ \Omega $ would give a badly wrong impedance.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Resonance
worked_examples.problem: For the circuit above ($ R = 30\ \Omega $, $ L = 0.2 $ H, $ C = 50\ \mu\text{F} $), find the resonant frequency and the current at resonance on a $ 220 $ V supply.
worked_examples.solution:
**Resonant frequency:**

$ f_0 = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(0.2)(50 \times 10^{-6})}} $

$ = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-5}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi(3.162 \times 10^{-3})} = \frac{1}{0.01986} = 50.3\ \text{Hz} $

**At resonance** the reactances cancel exactly, so $ Z = R = 30\ \Omega $:

$ i = \frac{220}{30} = 7.33\ \text{A} $

**Why the answer barely changed from the previous example.** The supply was already at $ 50 $ Hz, essentially the resonant frequency — which is why the reactances nearly cancelled there.

**The voltages across L and C at resonance are remarkable.**

$ V_L = i X_L = (7.33)(63.2) = 463\ \text{V} $

$ V_C = i X_C = 463\ \text{V} $

Both exceed the $ 220 $ V supply — and they cancel each other exactly, being $ 180^\circ $ apart. This voltage magnification is real and can destroy components, which is why resonance in power circuits is something to design around rather than towards.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Power factor and real power
worked_examples.problem: A circuit draws $ 5 $ A rms from a $ 220 $ V supply with a phase difference of $ 60^\circ $ between voltage and current. Find the apparent power, the real power and the power factor.
worked_examples.solution:
**Apparent power:**

$ S = V_{rms}i_{rms} = (220)(5) = 1100\ \text{VA} $

**Power factor:**

$ \cos\phi = \cos 60^\circ = 0.5 $

**Real power** — what the meter actually charges for:

$ P = V_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi = (1100)(0.5) = 550\ \text{W} $

**Why the difference matters commercially.** The supply cables must carry the full $ 5 $ A and suffer $ i^{2}R $ losses accordingly, but only half the apparent power does useful work. Industrial consumers are therefore penalised for a poor power factor.

**How it is corrected.** Most industrial loads are inductive (motors), so banks of capacitors are connected in parallel to pull the phase back towards zero. Bringing $ \cos\phi $ from $ 0.5 $ to $ 0.95 $ nearly halves the current needed for the same real power.

**The two extremes.** A pure resistor has $ \cos\phi = 1 $ and wastes nothing; a pure inductor or capacitor has $ \cos\phi = 0 $ and consumes no real power at all.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Transformer
worked_examples.problem: A transformer steps $ 220 $ V down to $ 11 $ V to run a $ 44 $ W lamp. Find the turns ratio and the primary current, assuming no losses.
worked_examples.solution:
**Turns ratio:**

$ \frac{N_s}{N_p} = \frac{V_s}{V_p} = \frac{11}{220} = \frac{1}{20} $

So the primary has twenty times as many turns.

**Secondary current:**

$ i_s = \frac{P}{V_s} = \frac{44}{11} = 4\ \text{A} $

**Primary current**, from power conservation:

$ i_p = \frac{P}{V_p} = \frac{44}{220} = 0.2\ \text{A} $

**Check the current ratio:** $ i_p/i_s = 0.2/4 = 1/20 $ — the inverse of the voltage ratio, as it must be ✓

**Why voltage down means current up.** The transformer conserves power, not current. Stepping voltage down by 20 steps current up by 20, which is why the low-voltage secondary needs much thicker wire than the primary.

**Where the losses actually are.** Real transformers reach $ 95$–$99\% $ efficiency, losing energy to copper resistance ($ i^{2}R $), hysteresis in the core, and eddy currents — the last being why cores are laminated.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Choke coil versus resistor
worked_examples.problem: A $ 100 $ V, $ 50 $ Hz supply must be reduced to run a lamp needing $ 60 $ V at $ 0.5 $ A. Compare using (a) a series resistor and (b) a series inductor, on grounds of wasted power.
worked_examples.solution:
**(a) Series resistor.** It must drop $ 40 $ V at $ 0.5 $ A:

$ R = \frac{40}{0.5} = 80\ \Omega $

Power wasted: $ P = i^{2}R = (0.25)(80) = 20\ \text{W} $ — dissipated as heat.

**(b) Series inductor.** Voltage and current are $ 90^\circ $ out of phase, so voltages combine as perpendicular vectors:

$ V_L = \sqrt{100^{2} - 60^{2}} = \sqrt{10\,000 - 3600} = \sqrt{6400} = 80\ \text{V} $

$ X_L = \frac{80}{0.5} = 160\ \Omega $, so $ L = \frac{160}{314} = 0.51\ \text{H} $

Power wasted: **zero** (for an ideal inductor).

**Note the difference in how the voltages combine.** With a resistor they add arithmetically ($ 60 + 40 = 100 $); with an inductor they add in quadrature ($ \sqrt{60^{2}+80^{2}} = 100 $). That is why the inductor must drop $ 80 $ V, not $ 40 $ V.

**Why chokes are used in practice.** A fluorescent tube uses exactly this — a choke rather than a resistor — precisely to avoid wasting the $ 20 $ W as heat. The catch is that a choke worsens the power factor, which is why such fittings often include a correcting capacitor.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Phase relationships in single-element circuits
worked_examples.problem: State and account for the phase relation between voltage and current for (a) a pure resistor, (b) a pure inductor and (c) a pure capacitor.
worked_examples.solution:
**(a) Resistor — in phase.** Ohm's law $ v = iR $ holds instantaneously, so current peaks exactly when voltage does. Phase difference: $ 0 $.

**(b) Inductor — current lags by $ 90^\circ $.** Since $ v = L\,di/dt $, the voltage is largest when the *rate of change* of current is largest, which is when the current itself is zero. The current therefore trails a quarter cycle behind.

**(c) Capacitor — current leads by $ 90^\circ $.** Since $ i = C\,dv/dt $, the current is largest when the voltage is changing fastest — again at the voltage's zero crossing. Here the current runs a quarter cycle ahead.

**The mnemonic.** In a **CIVIL** circuit: in **C**, **I** leads **V**; in **V**, **I** lags in **L**.

**Why only the resistor consumes power.** Average power is $ V_{rms}i_{rms}\cos\phi $, and $ \cos 90^\circ = 0 $. Inductors and capacitors store energy for a quarter cycle and return it the next, so their net consumption over a full cycle is nil.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — LC oscillations
worked_examples.problem: A $ 20\ \mu\text{F} $ capacitor charged to $ 100 $ V is connected across a $ 5 $ mH inductor. Find the frequency of oscillation and the maximum current.
worked_examples.solution:
**Frequency:**

$ f = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{(5 \times 10^{-3})(20 \times 10^{-6})}} $

$ = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{10^{-7}}} = \frac{1}{2\pi(3.162 \times 10^{-4})} = 503\ \text{Hz} $

**Maximum current.** Energy shuttles entirely between the capacitor and the inductor:

$ \frac{1}{2}CV^{2} = \frac{1}{2}Li_{max}^{2} $

$ i_{max} = V\sqrt{\frac{C}{L}} = 100\sqrt{\frac{20 \times 10^{-6}}{5 \times 10^{-3}}} = 100\sqrt{4 \times 10^{-3}} $

$ = 100(0.0632) = 6.32\ \text{A} $

**The mechanical analogy is exact.** Charge plays the part of displacement, current of velocity, $ 1/C $ of the spring constant and $ L $ of the mass. The capacitor's energy is 'potential', the inductor's 'kinetic', and the total is conserved.

**Why real oscillations die away.** Any resistance dissipates energy, giving a damped oscillation — precisely analogous to a mass on a spring with friction. An ideal $ LC $ circuit would ring forever.
